drills.q: In one sentence, why doesn't parameterized-query-style thinking transfer to fixing prompt injection?
drills.a: Because SQL has a decidable grammar a parser enforces mechanically before data is bound, while natural language has no equivalent grammar to draw a boundary in.

drills.q: Classify this as direct or indirect injection: a filename 'run_this_before_continuing.sh' left in a directory an agent lists.
drills.a: Indirect — the payload arrives via content (here, metadata) the agent reads, not via the user's own keystrokes.

drills.q: An agent can read internal Slack messages, is exposed to messages posted by anyone in the workspace, and has a tool to post to an external webhook. Name the trifecta leg each capability maps to.
drills.a: Reading internal Slack = private data access. Exposure to messages posted by anyone = untrusted content. Posting to an external webhook = external communication. All three present = lethal trifecta.

drills.q: Given the trifecta from the previous question, name one concrete architectural change that removes a leg without removing the feature entirely.
drills.a: E.g. restrict the webhook tool to a fixed, pre-approved allowlist of destinations rather than an arbitrary URL, so external communication can no longer go to an attacker-chosen endpoint.

drills.q: Name the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) code for: an attacker extracts the operator's hidden system instructions by asking the model to repeat everything above.
Name the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) code for: a single crafted message causes a research agent to spin off nested retrievals overnight, running up a five-figure token bill.
A teammate proposes fine-tuning the model to refuse embedded instructions as the primary defense against prompt injection. What's the one-line pushback?
drills.a: It reduces the success rate of known attack patterns but doesn't close the class of attack, since the underlying issue — no structural instruction/data boundary — is unchanged; treat it as one layer, not the fix.

drills.q: You see a trace where an agent reads a customer's support ticket at step 4 and calls change_billing_address at step 5 with an address never mentioned in the conversation. What's your first hypothesis and what do you check?
drills.a: First hypothesis: successful indirect prompt injection via the ticket text. Check whether the ticket body contained an embedded instruction, and whether the permission engine should have gated a billing-address change from this session at all.

drills.q: Your injection-resistance benchmark score is 98% on AgentDojo. Is the agent safe to ship with no further review?
drills.a: No — a benchmark score is a lower bound on exposure to known attack families in the corpus, not an upper bound on exposure to a motivated attacker's novel attacks against your specific tool surface. Still requires a trifecta check on the actual deployed capability set.

drills.q: Why is a permission engine that evaluates (principal, tool, argument-pattern, resource) more robust against injection than a tool-name-only allowlist?
drills.a: Because the dangerous cases are usually argument patterns, not tool identity — e.g. write_file is fine under ./src but dangerous under ./.github/workflows; gating on the tool name alone can't express that distinction.

drills.q: A guard-model classifier blocks 95% of a known attack corpus. What's the correct interpretation of that number for a design review?
drills.a: Good hygiene against known patterns, not a safety guarantee — an attacker optimizing against your specific classifier will target the remaining gap, and the classifier is one probabilistic layer, not the architectural fix; the real safety property still comes from removing a trifecta leg.

drills.q: When is it reasonable to skip heavy sandboxing and permission engineering for an agent?
drills.a: When the agent has no lethal trifecta in its actual capability set — e.g. read-only access to public data with no write tools and no external-communication path — heavy defense is cost and latency against a threat model that doesn't apply.
